Why Choose Karakoram Backpackers?

At Karakoram Backpackers, we offer unforgettable adventures across Northern Pakistan, from K2 Basecamp to Fairy Meadows and Deosai Plains. With expert local guides and seamless logistics, we ensure a hassle-free experience for all travelers.

We prioritize eco-friendly tourism, practicing zero-waste camping, and supporting local communities through Home stays. With trusted accommodations and transport partners, we make every journey smooth, enriching, and truly unforgettable. Join us for life time memories and thrilling adventures.

Expert Guides

Karakoram Backpackers is an adventure travel company based in Gilgit Baltistan. We specialize in customized tours across northern Pakistan and focus on sustainable tourism, offering authentic experiences in the Karakoram, Hindukush, and Himalayas.

Our team of experts ensures safe, enriching trips, connecting travelers with the region's natural beauty and culture.

Fairy Meadows

The Gateway to Nanga Parbat

Why is Fairy Meadows So Special?

Fairy Meadows, locally known as "Joot," is one of Pakistan’s most breathtaking destinations—a lush alpine meadow nestled at 3,300 meters (10,827 ft) at the base of Nanga Parbat (8,126m), the world’s 9th highest peak and famously called the "Killer Mountain."

What Makes Fairy Meadows Unique?

✔ Unmatched Scenery – A carpet of wildflowers, dense pine forests, and jaw-dropping views of Nanga Parbat.
✔ One of the World’s Most Beautiful Campsites – Named by German climbers in the 1930s for its fairy-tale-like beauty.
✔ Gateway to Nanga Parbat Base Camp – A thrilling trek to the foot of one of the most dangerous mountains on Earth.
✔ Stargazing Paradise – With minimal light pollution, the night sky reveals the Milky Way in full glory.
✔ Cultural Richness – Meet the indigenous Raikot people, known for their hospitality.

Why Should You Visit Fairy Meadows?

✅ For Adventure Seekers – A moderate trek with rewarding views.
✅ For Photographers – Sunrise/sunset on Nanga Parbat is a dream shot.
✅ For Nature Lovers – Pristine landscapes, rare wildlife (Himalayan brown bears, snow leopards).
✅ For Solitude & Peace – Far from crowds, a true escape into wilderness.

382.title: 12 Days Complete tour of Gilgit, Skardu and fairymeadows
382.content:
12 days complete tour of gilgit baltistan

Why is Gilgit-Baltistan So Special?

Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) is a paradise for adventurers, nature lovers, and culture seekers, home to some of the world’s highest peaks, ancient Silk Road history, and breathtaking landscapes. Known as the "Land of Giants," it hosts:
✔ Five 8,000m+ peaks (K2, Nanga Parbat, Gasherbrum I & II, Broad Peak).
✔ The world’s largest glaciers (Biafo, Baltoro, Hispar).
✔ Stunning valleys (Hunza, Skardu, Shigar, Nagar).
✔ Rich cultural heritage (Balti, Wakhi, and Burusho communities).
✔ Adventure hub for trekking, mountaineering, and jeep safaris.

Why Should You Visit Gilgit-Baltistan?

✅ For Trekkers – Fairy Meadows, K2 Base Camp, Rush Lake.
✅ For Photographers – Turquoise lakes, golden peaks, starry skies.
✅ For History Buffs – Ancient forts, petroglyphs, Silk Road relics.
✅ For Peace Seekers – Remote villages, serene landscapes.

The road trip including Fairy Meadows trek

Discover the Majesty of Pakistan’s Northern Paradise

Embark on an unforgettable 12-day journey through Gilgit-Baltistan, a land of towering peaks, turquoise lakes, and ancient cultures. This all-inclusive tour takes you to the most breathtaking destinations, including the legendary Fairy Meadows & Nanga Parbat Base Camp, the serene Attabad Lake, the historic Baltit Fort, and the mesmerizing Deosai Plains.

Perfect for adventure seekers, nature lovers, and photographers, this expedition blends trekking, cultural immersion, and scenic road trips along the Karakoram Highway (KKH)—one of the world’s most spectacular roads.

Start your journey with an adventurous road trip
heading towards the stunning valleys of northern
Pakistan. Drive on the beauty of the Karakoram
Highway, known as the world’s 8th wonder.
Morning:
8 am – Tour starts
Travel on the scenic Karakoram Highway to Batakundi
(9 hours).
Afternoon: - Scenic drive through through the Indus Valley on the
Karakoram Highway, known as the world’s 8th
wonder. - Stop at Naran, an alpine town in the Kaghan Valley,
for exploration and breathtaking views.
Evening:
Arrive in Batakundi, a town surrounded by rugged
mountains and rivers.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle
Accommodation: Guesthouse in Batakundi

Day 2: Batakundi – Fairy Meadows

Continue your journey to one of the most stunning
alpine meadows in the world, Fairy Meadows, located
at the base of the mighty Nanga Parbat, the 9th
highest mountain in the world.
Morning: - Travel to Raikot Bridge on the Karakoram Highway
(2 hours). - Transfer to a 4x4 vehicle and continue to Tatu Village
(2 hours). - Explore the picturesque Tatu Village in the Gilgit
Baltistan region.
Afternoon: - Begin the trek from Tatu Village to Fairy Meadows
(3 hours, 6 km, elevation gain: 300m). -Arrive at Fairy Meadows, a lush alpine pasture with
incredible views of Nanga Parbat.
Evening: - Set up tents and enjoy an evening surrounded by
majestic peaks and serene nature.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle
Accommodation: Camping at Fairy Meadows

Day 3: Fairy Meadows – Biyal Base Camp

Immerse yourself in nature as you hike through the
breathtaking scenery of Fairy Meadows toward Biyal
Camp, closer to Nanga Parbat Base Camp.
Morning: - Begin the hike from Fairy Meadows to Biyal Camp
(2 hours, 3 km, elevation gain: 75m). - Visit local villages and towns along the trekking
route.
Afternoon: - Explore the hiking trail with panoramic views of
Nanga Parbat, glaciers, and forests. - Enjoy leisure activities like cricket with the locals,
making your adventure memorable. Explore local
villages to gain insights into life in this remote region.
Evening: - Overnight camping under the stars at Biyal Camp.
Accommodation: Camping at Biyal Camp.

Day 4: Biyal Camp – Fairy Meadows – Gilgit

Conclude your trekking adventure with a scenic
descent from Fairy Meadows and travel to Gilgit, the
heart of Gilgit-Baltistan.
Morning:
Hike back to Fairy Meadows and the park’s main
entrance (3 hours, 8 km, elevation loss: 300m).
Afternoon:
Travel from Fairy Meadows to Gilgit (3–4 hours),
enjoying the beautiful landscapes along the way.
Evening:
Immerse yourself in local life with a local homestay in
Gilgit, surrounded by mountain views and local
hospitality.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle
Accommodation: Homestay at Gilgit or Hotel 

Day 5: Gilgit – Karimabad (Hunza Valley)

Journey into the heart of the Hunza Valley, known for
its breathtaking natural beauty, vibrant culture, and
welcoming communities.
Morning: - Visit the Junction Point of Three Mountain Ranges,
where the Karakoram, Himalayas, and Hindu Kush
meet. - Explore the vibrant Gilgit Bazaar, famous for its
woolen traditional attire.
Afternoon: - Travel to Hunza Valley in the Karakoram Range
(3 hours) - Stop at villages of the Brusho and Shinaki people,
renowned for their distinct identities and traditions.
Evening:
Arrive in Karimabad, the capital of Hunza Valley.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle
Accommodation: Guesthouse in Karimabad

Day 6: Hunza Valley & Passu Mountains

Discover the architectural marvels, jagged peaks, and
serene lakes of the Hunza Valley.
Morning: - Visit the Altit Fort (12th century) and Baltit Fort (14th
century), both UNESCO World Heritage Sites. - Appreciate the unique Himalayan and Tibetan
architectural styles.
Afternoon: - Travel toward the Passu Cones, sharp jagged peaks of
the Hunza Valley. - Stop at Attabad Lake, formed by a massive landslide
in 2010, for a short hike. - Cross the Passu Suspension Bridge, a local landmark
and engineering feat, and visit nearby glaciers.
Evening:
Return to Karimabad for the night.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle
Accommodation: Guesthouse in Karimabad

Day 7: Hunza Valley – Gilgit

Continue along the Karakoram Highway, exploring
ancient rock carvings and glaciers before arriving in
Gilgit.
Morning: - Travel back toward Gilgit via the Karakoram Highway
(3 hours) - Stop at Ganish Bridge and view the 8th-century
Manthal Buddha Rock Carvings.
Afternoon: - Explore the Rakaposhi Glaciers, one of the world’s
largest non-polar glaciers. - Cross the Danyore Suspension Bridge, offering
stunning views of the surrounding landscapes. - Visit the Kargah Buddha, a 7th-century rock carving,
a testament to Buddhism once rich influence in the
region.
Evening:
Arrive in Gilgit and stay overnight at a local homestay.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle
Accommodation: Homestay in Gilgit or Hotel

Day 8: Gilgit – Skardu (Karakoram JSR) road

Travel along the stunning Jaglot-Skardu Road, known
for breathtaking mountain views, deep valleys, and
rugged landscapes, to reach the serene and culturally
rich town of Skardu
Morning:
Drive along the scenic Jaglot-Skardu Road (4 hours).
Afternoon: - Visit the Skardu Shangrila Resort, famously known as
"Heaven on Earth," for its serene landscapes. - Explore Upper Kachura Lake, with an optional zipline
or boating experience (additional fee).
Evening: - Discover the town of Skardu, renowned for its
breathtaking landscapes and rich cultural heritage.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle
Accommodation: Homestay in Skardu

Day 9: Skardu & surroundings

Explore Skardu’s historical and natural wonders,
including ancient forts, crystal-clear lakes, serene
valleys, and golden sand dunes, offering a perfect
blend of adventure, history, and scenic beauty.
Morning:
Travel to Kharpocho Fort (3 hours), a 16th-century fort
with panoramic views of the Indus and Skardu Valleys.
Afternoon: - Visit the Shigar Valley and Blind Lake, a crystal-clear
lake surrounded by mountains. - Experience a desert safari in the Shigar Valley, with
optional ATV and bike rides (additional fee).
Evening: - Return to Skardu for the night.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle
Accommodation: Homestay in Skardu or Guest House 

Day 10: Return to Islamabad

Conclude your adventure with a scenic journey back to
Islamabad, either by flight or road. Reflect on the
breathtaking landscapes and cultural experiences from
this unforgettable exploration of northern Pakistan.
Morning:
Fly from Skardu to Islamabad (1 hour)
Or
Travel by road to Gilgit (4 hours) and then to
Islamabad by flight (1 hour).
Depends on weather & airline schedules
Afternoon: - Arrive in Islamabad. - If time permits, enjoy a short city tour.
Evening:
Tour ends at 6 PM.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle, Plane

Islamabad, either by flight or road. Reflect on the
breathtaking landscapes and cultural experiences from
this unforgettable exploration of northern Pakistan.

Or
Travel by road to Gilgit (4 hours) and then to
Islamabad by flight (1 hour).
Depends on weather & airline schedules

Evening:
Tour ends at 6 PM.
Transportation: Private-hire vehicle, Plane

🏔️ History of Shimshal Valley & Amazing Facts

📜 Ancient Origins & Cultural Heritage

Shimshal Valley, located in the Karakoram Mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan, is one of Pakistan’s most remote and breathtaking regions. It is home to the Wakhi people, an ethnic group known for their semi-nomadic lifestyle and deep connection to the mountains.

  • Historical Significance:

    • Part of the Silk Route – Shimshal was a key passage for traders traveling between China and Central Asia.

    • Wakhi Traditions – The valley has preserved its animal herding (yaks, goats) and polo culture for centuries.

    • British Exploration – Early 20th-century explorers used Shimshal as a gateway to K2 and other Karakoram peaks.

🌍 Amazing Facts About Shimshal

✅ Highest Pass: Shimshal Pass (4,735m) – A historic trade route to China.
✅ Adventure Hub: Gateway to treks like Shimshal Pamir and Minglik Sar.
✅ Unique Wildlife: Home to snow leopards, ibex, and Marco Polo sheep.
✅ No Roads Until 2003! – Shimshal was only accessible by foot or horseback before the Shimshal Road was built.
✅ Women Polo Players – Shimshal is famous for its female yak polo teams!

🎉 Shimshal Kuch Festival: A Celebration of Wakhi Culture

Held annually in July or August, this festival celebrates mountain life, yak herding, and Wakhi traditions.

🎪 Festival Highlights:

  • 🐎 Yak & Horse Polo – A rugged, high-altitude version of polo.

  • 🎶 Wakhi Music & Dance – Traditional instruments like the daf (drum) and rubab.

  • 🏔️ Trekking & Camping – Explore the Shimshal Pamir (high-altitude pastures).

  • 🥘 Local Food – Try Shir Chai (salt tea), Chapshuro (meat bread), and dried fruits.

Kelash valley

The Kalash Valley, located in the remote mountains of Chitral District, Pakistan, is home to the Kalash people, one of the world’s most unique and culturally preserved indigenous communities. The Kalash are often referred to as the "Last Pagans of the Hindu Kush" due to their ancient polytheistic religion, which stands in contrast to the predominantly Muslim population of Pakistan.

Origins & Ancient Connections

The origins of the Kalash people remain a subject of debate, but many historians and anthropologists believe they may be descendants of Alexander the Great’s army, which passed through this region in 326 BCE. Some Kalash claim lineage from Greek soldiers who settled here, supported by their light skin, blue or green eyes, and distinct cultural practices. However, genetic studies suggest a mix of Indo-Aryan, Greek, and Central Asian ancestry.

Before the arrival of Islam in the region, the Kalash practiced an animist religion, worshipping nature spirits and a pantheon of gods. Their faith centers around Dezau (the supreme god), along with other deities linked to mountains, rivers, and fertility.

Islamic Influence & Cultural Survival

Over the centuries, the Kalash faced gradual conversion pressures from neighboring Muslim communities. By the 19th century, many Kalash were forced to convert to Islam, reducing their numbers significantly. Today, only around 3,000-4,000 Kalash remain, concentrated in three main valleys: Bumburet, Rumbur, and Birir.

Despite external influences, the Kalash have fiercely preserved their traditions, including their language (Kalasha), festivals, and unique way of life. Their resistance to assimilation makes them a living anthropological treasure.

The Chilam Joshi Festival: A Celebration of Spring & Fertility

The Chilam Joshi Festival is one of the most vibrant and significant cultural events in the Kalash calendar. Held every year in mid-May, it marks the arrival of spring, a time for renewal, fertility, and matchmaking.

Religious & Cultural Significance

The festival is dedicated to the gods and goddesses of the Kalash pantheon, particularly Jestak (the goddess of home and family) and Dezau (the creator god). The Kalash believe that celebrating Chilam Joshi ensures good harvests, healthy livestock, and strong family bonds for the coming year.

Rituals & Celebrations

  1. Preparation & Purification

    • Before the festival, Kalash women clean their homes and decorate them with fresh flowers and walnut branches.

    • Men prepare sacrificial goats as offerings to the gods.

  2. Traditional Attire & Dance

    • Women wear elaborate black woolen dresses adorned with colorful beads, cowrie shells, and intricate embroidery.

    • Men dress in traditional shalwar kameez with woolen vests and join in the drum-and-flute dances.

  3. Sacrificial Offerings & Prayers

    • A goat or sheep is sacrificed, and its blood is sprinkled on sacred altars to seek blessings.

    • The Kalash pray for prosperity and perform rituals near their Jestak Han (temple of the goddess Jestak).

  4. Matchmaking & Wine Drinking

    • Unmarried men and women participate in group dances, where romantic connections are often made.

    • Mulberry wine (called "Tara") is shared freely, as alcohol is a sacred part of Kalash rituals.

Unique Customs

  • Proposal by Bread-Throwing: If a Kalash woman is interested in a man, she may throw bread at him during the dance—a playful yet serious marriage proposal!

  • Spiritual Cleansing: Villagers believe that the festival washes away evil spirits and brings good fortune.

Why Chilam Joshi is a Must-See Festival

The Chilam Joshi Festival offers a rare glimpse into a prehistoric culture that has survived against all odds. Unlike mainstream Islamic festivals in Pakistan, Chilam Joshi is filled with music, dance, wine, and pagan rituals, making it a once-in-a-lifetime experience for travelers.
